name: The Josephson Effect
statement: A supercurrent of Cooper pairs can tunnel between two superconductors separated by a thin barrier, even with zero applied voltage.
statementAccent: tunnel between two superconductors separated by a thin barrier
meaning: The Josephson effect describes quantum tunnelling of superconducting Cooper pairs — not single electrons — across a weak link joining two superconductors. It manifests as a DC supercurrent with no voltage drop, and as an oscillating AC current when a fixed voltage is applied.
mechanism: The macroscopic quantum phases of the two superconducting condensates are coupled across the barrier, giving a current-phase relation in which the supercurrent is the critical current times the sine of the phase difference. Under an applied voltage the phase evolves at a rate proportional to the voltage, producing an oscillating current (the AC Josephson effect); conversely, microwave irradiation locks the junction to quantised DC voltage steps.

examples.text: Superconducting quantum interference devices use loops containing Josephson junctions to detect extremely small magnetic fields via flux-dependent interference of the junction currents.
Arrays of tens of thousands of Josephson junctions irradiated with microwaves produce exactly quantised voltage steps, used as the international standard for the volt.
Josephson junctions provide the nonlinear, non-dissipative inductance needed to build the superconducting qubits used in quantum computers.

whyItMatters: The effect enables the most precise electrical measurement standards in existence and underlies essentially all superconducting quantum-computing hardware. It also gave direct macroscopic evidence for quantum phase coherence, a cornerstone confirmation of BCS superconductivity theory.
limits: The effect requires the barrier to be thin enough (typically nanometres) for Cooper-pair tunnelling and both electrodes to be superconducting below their critical temperature. Thermal noise, magnetic fields, and quasiparticle excitations can suppress the supercurrent, and the simple sinusoidal current-phase relation is an idealisation.
misreadings: It is a common error to think the DC Josephson effect requires an applied voltage to drive current — the defining feature is current flow at exactly zero voltage; voltage only appears in the distinct AC Josephson effect.
origin: Predicted by Brian Josephson in 1962 as a 22-year-old PhD student at Cambridge; he shared the 1973 Nobel Prize in Physics (with Leo Esaki and Ivar Giaever) for the discovery.
